items.definition: to stop sleeping and become awake
exampleSentences: I always wake up before my alarm rings.
She wakes up at six every morning.
Do you usually wake up early on weekends?

items.definition: to leave your bed after waking up
exampleSentences: I get up as soon as my alarm rings.
He gets up at seven every weekday.
We usually get up early to catch the bus.

items.definition: a clock that makes a sound to wake you up at a certain time
exampleSentences: My alarm clock rings at six thirty.
She sets her alarm clock before she goes to sleep.
His alarm clock is too quiet to wake him up.

items.definition: to put on your clothes
exampleSentences: I get dressed right after my shower.
He gets dressed quickly every morning.
The children get dressed by themselves now.

items.definition: to clean something with a brush, especially your teeth or hair
exampleSentences: I brush my teeth twice a day.
She brushes her hair before school.
Don't forget to brush your teeth before bed.

items.definition: an act of washing your whole body while standing under running water
exampleSentences: I take a shower every morning before work.
She showers quickly when she's in a rush.
He always showers after he exercises.

items.definition: the first meal of the day, usually eaten in the morning
exampleSentences: I never skip breakfast on weekdays.
She eats breakfast at seven every morning.
We had a big breakfast before the trip.

items.definition: to hurry because you do not have much time
exampleSentences: I always rush to catch the morning bus.
She rushed out of the house without her keys.
There's no need to rush; we have plenty of time.

items.definition: not late; at the correct or expected time
exampleSentences: The bus is usually on time in the morning.
I try to arrive on time for work every day.
She is always on time for meetings.

items.definition: to travel regularly between home and work
exampleSentences: I commute to the city center every day.
She commutes by train for about an hour.
Many people commute long distances for work.

items.definition: a short period of time during the working day when you stop to eat lunch
exampleSentences: I usually go for a walk during my lunch break.
Her lunch break is only thirty minutes long.
We often eat together on our lunch break.

items.definition: a small job that you do regularly, especially around the house
exampleSentences: I do household chores every Saturday morning.
Washing the dishes is my least favorite chore.
The children help with chores after school.

items.definition: clothes that need to be washed, or the activity of washing them
exampleSentences: I do the laundry every Sunday evening.
She hung the laundry outside to dry.
He never has time to do his laundry during the week.

items.definition: food and other things for the home that you buy regularly in a store; often used in the plural
exampleSentences: I buy groceries every Friday after work.
There's a small grocery store at the end of my street.
We ran out of groceries, so I need to shop today.

items.definition: a short trip you make to do a small job, like going to the post office or picking up medicine
exampleSentences: I have a few errands to run this afternoon.
She ran an errand to the pharmacy before lunch.
We usually do our errands together on Saturdays.

items.definition: extremely tired
exampleSentences: I feel exhausted after a long day at work.
She was exhausted when she finally got home.
He looked exhausted after the long commute.

items.definition: to arrive at your house or apartment
exampleSentences: I usually get home around six in the evening.
She gets home late on Fridays because of traffic.
By the time we get home, it's already dark.

items.definition: to rest and stop worrying or working
exampleSentences: I like to relax on the sofa after dinner.
She relaxes by reading before bed.
We relaxed all weekend and did nothing special.

items.definition: a short sleep, usually during the day
exampleSentences: I sometimes take a nap after lunch.
She naps for twenty minutes every afternoon.
A short nap can help you feel more awake.

items.definition: the time when you usually go to bed
exampleSentences: Bedtime for the kids is eight o'clock.
I read a book before bedtime every night.
Her bedtime routine includes brushing her teeth and reading.

items.definition: a regular way of doing things, in a particular order
exampleSentences: My morning routine never really changes.
He has a strict evening routine before bed.
Their daily routine includes a short walk after dinner.

items.definition: a plan that shows when things will happen or when someone will do things
exampleSentences: My work schedule changes every week.
She keeps a busy schedule during the school year.
We planned our schedule for the whole month.

items.definition: any day except Saturday and Sunday
exampleSentences: I get up early on weekdays.
The store is open until nine on weekdays.
We rarely go out for dinner on a weekday.

items.definition: Saturday and Sunday, the days when many people do not work
exampleSentences: I usually sleep in on the weekend.
We visit my parents most weekends.
Her weekend plans include hiking and reading.

items.definition: most of the time; almost always
exampleSentences: I usually walk to work when the weather is nice.
She usually has coffee for breakfast.
They usually spend weekends with family.

items.definition: many times; frequently
exampleSentences: I often forget to eat breakfast.
She often works late on Fridays.
We don't often go to the cinema.

items.definition: on some occasions but not always
exampleSentences: I sometimes skip breakfast when I'm in a hurry.
She sometimes takes the bus instead of driving.
We sometimes eat out on Fridays.

items.definition: not often; only a few times
exampleSentences: I rarely eat fast food these days.
She rarely complains about her job.
We rarely see snow in this city.

items.definition: at all times; every time
exampleSentences: I always brush my teeth before bed.
She always arrives early for work.
We always eat dinner together as a family.

items.definition: not at any time; not once
exampleSentences: I never eat breakfast before seven.
She never misses her morning run.
We never go out on weeknights.

lessons.title: Grammar: Present simple with adverbs of frequency

items.headword: Present simple with adverbs of frequency
items.definition: how to use words like always, usually, and never with the present simple
items.explanationTR:
We use the present simple to talk about habits, routines, and things that are generally true. Adverbs of frequency tell us how often something happens.

Common adverbs of frequency, from 100% to 0%:
• always
• usually
• often
• sometimes
• rarely / hardly ever
• never

Word order:
• Before the main verb: She usually wakes up at seven.
• After the verb 'be': He is always on time.
• 'Sometimes' and 'usually' can also start a sentence: Sometimes I skip breakfast.

Questions with frequency:
• How often do you check your email? — I check it every hour.

Don't forget the regular present simple rules: add -s or -es for he/she/it (she watches, he brushes his teeth), and use don't/doesn't for negatives and do/does for questions. For example: Does she usually cook dinner? No, she doesn't usually cook on weekdays.

questions.prompt: We ---- go to the gym on Saturday mornings.
questions.explanationTR: Adverbs of frequency like "usually" go before the main verb in the present simple ("we usually go"); no form of "be" is needed here because "go" is already the main verb.

questions.prompt: The train ---- late, so I always get to work on time.
questions.explanationTR: With the verb "be," the frequency adverb comes right after "is/am/are" ("is never late"); "never" already means "not ever," so adding "not" or "doesn't" would create a double negative.

questions.prompt: A: ---- do you check your phone in the morning? B: About three times, I think.
questions.explanationTR: "How often" asks about frequency and matches the answer "about three times"; "how much" and "how many" ask about quantity, not frequency.

questions.prompt: He ---- eats vegetables; he only likes pizza and burgers.
questions.explanationTR: "Hardly ever" (almost never) goes before the main verb in the present simple, just like "never" and "rarely"; no extra "does" or "is" is needed in this affirmative sentence.

questions.prompt: ---- I skip breakfast, but most days I eat something small before work.
questions.explanationTR: "Sometimes" is one of the few frequency adverbs that can start a sentence, and it means "occasionally," which fits the contrast with "most days I eat something"; "often," "usually," and "always" would all contradict that contrast.

questions.prompt: My sister ---- to music while she cooks dinner.
questions.explanationTR: Third-person singular subjects like "she" need "-s" on the verb in the present simple ("she usually listens"), and the adverb still goes before the verb.

questions.prompt: I ---- eat fast food; maybe once or twice a year.
questions.explanationTR: "Rarely" already has a negative meaning ("almost never"), so it is not combined with "don't"; it simply goes before the main verb.

questions.prompt: They ---- watch TV after dinner; it's part of their evening routine.
questions.explanationTR: "Always" goes directly before the main verb ("they always watch"); no extra auxiliary like "does" or "is" is needed in this affirmative present simple sentence.

items.definition: Short dialogues about everyday routines and eight questions about what to say next

questions.prompt:
A: Do you usually walk to work?
B: ----
A: That makes sense. The bus is much faster, too.
options: Yes, I never eat breakfast before work.
No, I don't like coffee in the morning.
No, I usually take the bus because it's too far to walk.
Yes, I always do my laundry on Sundays.
No, I finished my homework already.
questions.explanationTR: The reply must answer the yes/no question about walking to work; A's "That makes sense" and the mention of the bus only fit a reply saying B takes the bus because walking is too far.

questions.prompt:
A: What time do you usually get up on weekdays?
B: ----
A: Wow, that's early! I usually get up at eight.
options: I usually have a sandwich for lunch.
I go to bed at eleven every night.
I don't like waking up early.
I get up at six, so I have time for breakfast.
questions.explanationTR: The question asks for a specific time, and only this option gives a time, which matches A's reaction, "that's early."

questions.prompt:
A: You look tired today.
B: ----
A: That sounds exhausting. You should try to relax tonight.
options: I always have cereal for breakfast.
I didn't sleep much last night because of work.
I usually take the train to the office.
I love spicy food for dinner.
questions.explanationTR: This option explains why the speaker looks tired, matching A's sympathetic follow-up about relaxing tonight; the other options don't answer why B looks tired.

questions.prompt:
A: Do you have a lunch break at your job?
B: ----
A: That's not much time to eat and relax.
options: No, I never do chores on weekdays.
Yes, I usually cook dinner at seven.
No, I take a shower every morning.
Yes, but it's only thirty minutes.
Yes, I always wake up at six.
questions.explanationTR: This option confirms there is a lunch break and gives its short length, which matches A's comment that it "is not much time."

questions.prompt:
A: What do you usually do after you get home from work?
B: ----
A: That sounds like a nice way to end the day.
options: I usually cook dinner and then relax on the sofa.
I get up early and go for a run.
I take the bus to work every day.
I brush my teeth twice a day.
I have a meeting every Monday morning.
questions.explanationTR: The question asks about the routine after coming home, and this is the only option describing an after-work evening activity, matching A's positive reaction.

questions.prompt:
A: Do you do the laundry on weekends?
B: ----
A: Me too — Saturdays are perfect for chores.
options: No, I always have breakfast at home.
Yes, I often go to the gym after work.
No, my commute takes an hour.
Yes, I never miss the bus.
questions.explanationTR: This option confirms doing laundry and gives a specific weekend day, matching A's agreement that "Saturdays are perfect for chores."

questions.prompt:
A: How often do you cook dinner during the week?
B: ----
A: That's a lot of cooking!
options: I rarely eat breakfast before nine.
I usually take a nap on Sundays.
I never set my alarm clock.
I sometimes go shopping on Fridays.
I cook almost every night after work.
questions.explanationTR: "That's a lot of cooking" only makes sense as a reaction to frequent cooking, which this option describes with "almost every night."

questions.prompt:
A: You seem very busy every morning.
B: ----
A: No wonder you're always in a rush!
options: I usually relax on the sofa after dinner.
I have to get up, shower, and get dressed in twenty minutes.
I take a long nap every afternoon.
I go to bed early on Sundays.
questions.explanationTR: This option explains why the person is "always in a rush" by describing a very short morning routine, which directly matches A's remark.
